motion: Can we be good without God?

bridges.description: Objective moral judgments can be reached through fallible public reasoning about harms, reciprocity, autonomy, and human nature without treating divine command as their necessary ground.
Interchangeable perspectives and individual autonomy generalize protections beyond local groups and support universal rights.
Historical moral change and durable preference for freedom provide defeasible evidence that inquiry can converge on better moral arrangements.
Objective obligation and equal human dignity fit a theological reality in which God authoritatively values humanity.
Creation and incarnation supply a common human nature and a basis for extending worth to every person, including the weak and outsiders.
Christian scripture, institutions, and moral imagination historically formed the rights and equality language now used in secular settings.

sections.title: Moral reality and secular reason
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether objective moral obligation requires God or can be grounded through fallible public reason.

sections.title: Genealogy of rights and moral reform
sections.rationale: The speakers contest Christian institutional contributions to abolition, medieval rights language, and continuing post-Christian values.

sections.title: Rights authority and Enlightenment foundations
sections.rationale: A focused exchange tests the eighteenth-century secular-rights claim, the need for nonarbitrary authority, and Franklin's rationalizing edit.

sections.title: Equal human worth and rights
sections.rationale: A central dispute concerns why every individual counts equally and how rights exist, are enforced, and extend beyond local groups.

sections.title: Scripture, Jesus, and shared humanity
sections.rationale: Distinct exchanges test whether biblical texts and the person of Jesus provide a clear basis for equality and universal human dignity.

sections.title: Evolution, cooperation, and outsiders
sections.rationale: The debate tests whether evolved cooperation supplies genuine morality and whether it reaches beyond kin and in-groups.

sections.title: Moral uncertainty and the future
sections.rationale: Late exchanges examine unresolved disputes, counterfactual belief changes, and each worldview's account of moral progress.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: we can know something about it
I think there are absolute rights and wrongs
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's opening question ends at event 59; Shermer then owns the continuous realism and fallibilism answer through event 88.
moves.importanceRationale: This states Shermer's basic objective yet fallibilist moral realism, which carries his motion-level burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It claims objective moral truth can be approached fallibly without revelation.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: There are objective moral truths even though human knowledge of them remains fallible and probabilistic.
moves.warrant: Reality is mind-independent and can be approached through evidence and probability despite human limitations.
moves.inference: Moral realism does not require claims of infallible access or divine revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Shermer's complete opening statement of realism, fallibilism, and their application to morality.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's really wrong whether there's a god or not
why not just give us the reasons
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's follow-up ends at event 99; Shermer then gives the continuous reasons-first answer through event 134.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Shermer's direct account of why God is unnecessary to moral justification.

burdenContact.rationale: It locates moral authority in reasons that remain valid regardless of a divine speaker.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Acts such as slavery or child abuse remain wrong regardless of whether God exists or commands otherwise.
moves.warrant: A rational moral agent needs the reasons why conduct should be endorsed or condemned; a divine instruction either has reasons that can be given or fails to settle the issue.
moves.inference: God adds no necessary justificatory step to moral judgment.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes the independence claim, the demand for reasons, and Shermer's initial historical application.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: We're living in a universe of right and wrong
moral truths that are real, that are objective
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale hands the floor to Scrivener before event 186; Scrivener owns the ontology argument through its capital-R conclusion at event 237.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Scrivener's opening motion-level response linking objective obligation to a theological ontology.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that real obligations are more expected in a theological than a matter-only reality.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener accepts Shermer's realism but disputes that its ontology is religiously neutral.
He answers the claim that God adds nothing by arguing that objective obligation itself points beyond matter in motion.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: A universe containing objective moral truths and obligations is already theological in character.
moves.warrant: Minds, abstract objects, beauty, and binding moral truths exceed a picture of reality exhausted by matter in motion.
moves.inference: Shermer's moral realism fits a theological universe better than the naturalism Scrivener attributes to the alternative.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Scrivener's answer and ends after his complete inference from objective wrongs to capital-R right, before he turns to separate historical claims.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: our modern building blocks for understanding what just war is
foundationally theological moral presuppositions
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener continues his own turn from metaphysics to historical examples at event 238 and completes the presuppositions claim at event 261.
moves.importanceRationale: The historical origin claim supports Scrivener's subsidiary genealogy burden and sets up the sustained dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies Christian sources for just war, abolition, dignity, equality, and rights.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Modern ideas such as just war, abolition, rights, dignity, and equality arose from Christian moral presuppositions.
moves.warrant: Scrivener cites Augustine and Christian action against ancient sexual exploitation and the slave trade as examples of theological ideas applied to social life.
moves.inference: The modern moral vocabulary is historically indebted to Christianity rather than an accidental product of naturalism.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Scrivener's transition to historical consequences and ends at his complete claim that the listed values are theological presuppositions.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: pro-slavery proponents were Christians
once the moral arc starts bending religions do get on board
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale requests Shermer's response at events 270–274; Shermer owns the ensuing pro-slavery and abolition reply through event 299.
moves.importanceRationale: This directly contests the claimed Christian ownership of abolition and moral reform.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats religious change as following broader moral reasoning rather than originating it.

responseComponents.description: Shermer counters Scrivener's Christian genealogy with Christian pro-slavery advocacy and later religious adaptation.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Christianity cannot claim sole credit for abolition because many Christians defended slavery and religious communities joined reform only after moral change was underway.
moves.warrant: Shermer points to nineteenth-century pro-slavery sermons and religious justifications alongside the minority Christian abolitionists.
moves.inference: Abolition is better explained by expanding moral reasoning than by Christianity alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Shermer's compact historical counterclaim immediately following Scrivener's opening genealogy.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: Does it apply to you and not just me
generalizability of a moral principle
moves.attributionRationale: After Scrivener's brief objection, Shermer resumes at event 304 and owns the generalizability argument through event 347.
moves.importanceRationale: Generalizability is a central secular mechanism for extending moral consideration.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds equal treatment in reciprocal, generalizable reasons rather than group membership.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: A sound moral principle must be interchangeable and generalizable across persons.
moves.warrant: If one would reject slavery or unequal treatment when positions are reversed, the same rule must apply to others; versions of the golden rule express this structure.
moves.inference: Reciprocal reasoning supports equal rights without requiring a uniquely Christian premise.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Shermer's secular formulation and ends at his complete conclusion that generalizability is the relevant moral principle; the following clipped continuation about other religions is unnecessary.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: why we can believe that every single human without exception
everybody in the human family counts
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener begins at event 352 after Shermer's sentence ends and owns the continuous equal-scope challenge through event 393.
moves.importanceRationale: This challenge isolates the debate's central unresolved question about equal scope.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks what within a secular system makes every human count equally, including the weak.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener accepts reciprocal reasoning but challenges its basis for counting every perspective equally.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Reciprocity alone does not explain why every human being's interests must count equally.
moves.warrant: Human beings differ in strength and social usefulness, and a society could claim aggregate benefit from excluding its weakest members.
moves.inference: Shermer needs a basis for universal equal membership rather than merely a procedure operating after membership is assumed.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Scrivener's own first words after Shermer's completed sentence and carries the challenge through the explicit weakest-person test.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: we don't want to live in a world
people can be sacrificed at any moment
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer explicitly accepts Scrivener's challenge at event 394 and owns the trolley and organ-harvesting contrast through event 431.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Shermer's distinct argument for an individual-protective constraint against aggregate sacrifice.

burdenContact.rationale: It links universal protections to autonomy and the general rejection of being sacrificed by a majority.

responseComponents.description: Shermer answers the equal-scope challenge with deontological limits, universal rights, and individual autonomy.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: A universal protection against sacrificing individuals cannot be reduced to simple aggregate utility.
moves.warrant: The trolley case can favor saving five over one, but generalizing that calculation to harvesting an innocent person's organs would make everyone vulnerable to majority whim.
moves.inference: Moral reasoning needs an individual-protective constraint in addition to outcome totals.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span isolates Shermer's trolley and organ-harvesting contrast through its majority-whim conclusion; the rolling final caption begins his separate historical transition, which is not used in this move.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: universal rights that apply to everybody no matter what
individual autonomy and control over your body
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer continues his own turn after the trolley example; events 432–483 contain his uninterrupted historical and philosophical rights-origin argument.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Shermer's distinct claim that universal rights were articulated through secular eighteenth-century reasoning and grounded in autonomy.

burdenContact.rationale: It links expanding moral inclusion to universal rights and bodily autonomy.

responseComponents.description: Shermer answers Scrivener's equal-scope challenge with an eighteenth-century universal-rights account and individual autonomy.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: The late eighteenth-century rights revolutions articulated universal rights through secular reasoning and placed individual autonomy at the start of the moral chain.
moves.warrant: Shermer says earlier societies accepted group favoritism, while the founding era generalized rights to everybody and later movements expanded the moral in-group.
moves.inference: Universal rights and bodily autonomy can be historically and philosophically grounded without treating revelation as their source.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span is Shermer's complete transition from the first rights revolution through moral-circle expansion to his autonomy conclusion; it is separate from the preceding trolley argument.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Gregorian reforms of the 11th century
reflection upon the image of God
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's question ends within event 517; Scrivener begins at event 518 and owns the dating and discovery argument through event 552.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies Scrivener's developed historical case for Christian rights language.

burdenContact.rationale: It traces rights to medieval canon law and scriptural anthropology rather than the Enlightenment alone.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener directly disputes Shermer's eighteenth-century dating and secular-origin claim with an eleventh-century Christian genealogy.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Human-rights language was first clearly articulated in eleventh-century Christian reforms as a discovery of a pre-existing moral reality.
moves.warrant: Scrivener contrasts Bentham's rejection of natural rights with Gregorian articulation rooted in the image of God and compares that articulation to Newton discovering an already existing force.
moves.inference: The relevant rights tradition predates the Enlightenment by centuries and arose within Christian theological reflection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage isolates Scrivener's dating and discovery claim; the later canon-law obligation-to-right mechanism is retained as its own move.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: someone from outside the system
The only thing self-evident about human rights
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener continues his uninterrupted response from the Declaration's language through the conclusion that rights are not self-evident; no other speaker occurs in events 553–622.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies Scrivener's positive warrant for why universal and equal rights need theological authority rather than assertion alone.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds nonarbitrary, unconditional, universal, and equal rights in an authoritative creator.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener directly contests Shermer's secular eighteenth-century origin by arguing that the Declaration's rights retain theological authority and are not self-evident.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Universal and equal human rights require nonarbitrary authority and are not self-evident products of human assertion.
moves.warrant: The Declaration describes rights as endowed by a creator; without an authority outside the system, a group's declaration of its own value is a power play, while creator-endowed rights remain unconditional across status and identity.
moves.inference: Franklin's language of self-evidence still operates within a theological account of universal equal worth.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span isolates Scrivener's authority argument from his earlier dating claim and carries it through the complete conclusion that rights arose through a Christian metaphysic.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: Franklin's edit instead turned it into an assertion of rationality
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer explicitly says he is quoting what he wrote, reads the Isaacson passage, and then states his own conclusion; the span contains no opponent or moderator speech.
moves.importanceRationale: The Franklin account supplies a distinct historical mechanism for treating equality as rational rather than sacred.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers an Enlightenment route by which equality was recast as publicly rational and self-evident.

responseComponents.description: Shermer replies to Scrivener's claim that Franklin's formulation remains theological by reading an account that describes the edit as an assertion of rationality.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Franklin's edit of Jefferson recast equality and rights from a sacred assertion into an assertion of rationality.
moves.warrant: Shermer reads Isaacson's account connecting self-evident truths to Newtonian and Humean rational traditions and contrasting Jefferson's word 'sacred' with Franklin's edit.
moves.inference: The American rights formulation has an identifiable rationalizing strand rather than being simply a direct statement of revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Shermer's explicit introduction of his quotation and ends with his own concise conclusion; later questions begin a separate exchange.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the poor person has a right
protecting the little guy
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener answers Shermer's source question continuously from canon-law collection through the obligation-to-right distinction; no host or opponent words occur in the selected span.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the concrete mechanism by which Scrivener says Christian obligation became enforceable rights language.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how scriptural first principles generated a claim held by the protected person against the powerful.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener answers Shermer's question about the source behind the earlier rights tradition with the canon-law derivation mechanism.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Medieval canon-law reasoning converted a giver's scriptural obligation into an enforceable right held by the poor person.
moves.warrant: Canon lawyers collected ecclesiastical decisions from scriptural first principles and recognized that the duty to provide has a corresponding claimant entitled to protection and provision.
moves.inference: Christian legal reasoning supplied a mechanism for rights that protect weak people against powerful structures.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Event 668 begins with Shermer's trailing word 'it?' and then Scrivener starts the canon-law answer; only Scrivener's words from 'So the canon lawyers' onward support this move, which continues through the obligation-right conversion and protective conclusion.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: that sounds like they're reasoning their way
Are there biblical passages you can cite
moves.attributionRationale: The transcript explicitly hands the floor to Shermer at event 722, and the selected span ends before Vitale's scheduling interjection.
moves.importanceRationale: The challenge distinguishes the use of reason by Christian institutions from proof that scripture supplied the rights conclusion.

burdenContact.rationale: It asks whether the described institutional process is rational inference and demands direct scriptural support for equality.

responseComponents.description: Shermer directly challenges whether Scrivener's canon-law mechanism shows reasoning rather than revelation and asks for its scriptural basis.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Scrivener's canon-law account sounds like people reasoning to rights conclusions, so a specifically biblical foundation still needs textual support.
moves.warrant: The described lawyers derive principles through case analysis; Shermer asks for passages stating equal treatment or universal rights.
moves.inference: Christian institutional participation does not by itself establish that the content came from revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Shermer's complete compact challenge and ends before the moderator limits the reply time.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: male and female, made in God's image
we are all one in Christ Jesus
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's time-limit interjection ends at event 734; Scrivener owns the complete short biblical answer at events 735–762.
moves.importanceRationale: This gives Scrivener's concise scriptural route from shared image to universal community.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds equal human status in creation and unity in Christ.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener directly answers Shermer's request for biblical passages by appealing to Genesis and unity in Christ.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Biblical theology treats humanity generally as bearing God's image and depicts a community transcending sex, status, and ethnicity.
moves.warrant: Genesis assigns royal image-bearing status to male and female, while unity in Christ makes slave and free, Jew and gentile members of one family.
moves.inference: Christian scripture provides a trajectory toward universal equal standing.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage is the full short answer identifying Genesis and unity in Christ as the requested scriptural trajectory.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the Christian presuppositions that we tend to have
detached those values from the Christian story
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale addresses Scrivener and ends at event 801; Scrivener owns the continuous post-Christian-values answer at events 802–882.
moves.importanceRationale: This develops the continuing-cultural component of Scrivener's genealogy beyond institutional belief.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that secular moral criticism retains Christian-shaped values after leaving their narrative source.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Post-Christian societies continue to moralize through values formed by Christianity even when those values are detached from their source.
moves.warrant: Equality, compassion, consent, enlightenment, science, freedom, and progress function as shared standards, including standards used to criticize churches.
moves.inference: Declining institutional Christianity does not show that contemporary morality is independent of Christian formation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete answer states the seven values, their use against churches, and the claimed consequence of detaching them from their story.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: don't I still have moral obligations
Because it hurts somebody else
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's prompt and handoff occupy events 883–892; Shermer's own answer begins at event 893 and continues through the completed reciprocity reason.
moves.importanceRationale: This directly states ordinary secular reasons for obligation after Scrivener's post-Christian diagnosis.

burdenContact.rationale: Harm, promises, and reciprocity supply reasons that persist without belief in God.

responseComponents.description: Shermer agrees that excessive moralizing exists but denies that moral obligations disappear without God.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Promises and duties not to harm others remain binding without God.
moves.warrant: Cheating and embezzlement hurt other people, violate commitments, and fail reciprocal treatment.
moves.inference: Recognizable moral obligations can be justified through interpersonal reasons rather than divine grounding.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The selected passage begins with Shermer's own response after the host handoff and carries his reciprocity reason through completion; the rolling final caption also begins his transition to the next biblical topic, which is not used here.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: yanked the passage out of context
you would have think the creator of the universe
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer explicitly introduces his Galatians argument and states the contextual conclusion in his own voice. The uncertain quoted commentary inside the span is not treated as Paul's words or as a citation error.
moves.importanceRationale: This is a distinct textual challenge to using Galatians as a foundation for universal rights.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a commonly offered biblical equality text concerns membership in Christ rather than an explicit general rights declaration.

responseComponents.description: Shermer challenges the use of Galatians in Scrivener's earlier scriptural trajectory by arguing that the surrounding context does not plainly declare universal civil rights.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Galatians 3:28 does not plainly function as an explicit declaration of universal human rights when read in its surrounding context.
moves.warrant: Shermer frames the passage as addressing entry into Christian identity across existing categories and observes that a creator intending universal rights could have stated them more forcefully.
moves.inference: The biblical text is not sufficient by itself to establish the claimed direct textual foundation for modern equal rights.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span retains Shermer's clear framing and contextual conclusion. Its internal quoted commentary is transcription-uncertain and is not used to allege misquotation or citation error.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: we've inculcated these values from many sources
individual is the target of selection
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener's direct question ends at event 1012; Shermer owns the response from event 1013 through the completed Dr. King sentence at event 1065.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Shermer's explicit answer to where equal individual worth enters his view.

burdenContact.rationale: It locates individualism in cultural inheritance, evolutionary selection, and anti-group political reasoning.

responseComponents.description: Shermer answers Scrivener's direct request for the source of inviolable individual worth.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Modern commitment to individual dignity comes from accumulated cultural sources and is reinforced by individual-level evolutionary and political reasoning.
moves.warrant: Values are transmitted through culture, families, peers, and literature; Shermer also treats individuals as the target of selection and invokes the political danger of prioritizing group identity.
moves.inference: Individual moral standing can have a natural and cultural source without requiring scriptural revelation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The answer begins with Shermer's direct response about the source of dignity and ends on the complete sentence invoking Dr. King's teaching, before the rolling captions enter a further paraphrase.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: their own political presuppositions
science wasn't really intended for that
moves.attributionRationale: Scrivener's substantive science-and-politics critique begins at event 1091 after the brief Shermer interjection and continues without another speaker through event 1142.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Scrivener's main challenge to deriving a preferred morality from science.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that empirical science cannot by itself authorize the moral and political values read into it.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener argues that Shermer's liberal individualism may be projected onto science rather than derived from it.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Attempts to derive morality from science risk projecting prior political commitments into scientific authority.
moves.warrant: Classical liberals, progressives, and scientific racists can each claim to see their preferred politics reflected in science.
moves.inference: Science should not be treated as independently yielding Shermer's liberal moral settlement.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins where Scrivener turns from biographical praise to the substantive examples of politicized science and ends with his complete warning about deriving a liberal settlement.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: the fullness of human knowledge
I can't act as if my interests are special
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer begins his reply at event 1143 and owns the continuous method and special-pleading argument through event 1207.
moves.importanceRationale: This clarifies Shermer's method and provides its central universalization argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Reason and the symmetry of justification constrain moral claims beyond narrow laboratory science.

responseComponents.description: Shermer clarifies that 'science' names broader rational inquiry and offers a reason-based constraint against special pleading.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Broad rational inquiry can discover moral constraints because a demand made of another cannot consistently privilege only the demander.
moves.warrant: Logic, empiricism, philosophy, and science together reveal that reasons must be stated in a form that applies equally when positions are reversed.
moves.inference: Universal moral conclusions can be reached without deriving values from a laboratory result alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Shermer's methodological clarification and uses his words through 'all-inclusive moral principles' in event 1208; the same rolling event ends with Vitale saying 'Michael,' to begin a new prompt, which supplies no scored evidence.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's actually more selfish for me to be selfless
I really genuinely do caring loving things
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's selflessness prompt ends at event 1220; Shermer owns the continuous evolutionary answer at events 1221–1273.
moves.importanceRationale: This answers whether evolutionary reciprocity can produce sincere rather than merely performed concern.

burdenContact.rationale: Evolved social mechanisms can stabilize felt altruism that supports cooperative moral life.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Reciprocal evolutionary pressures can produce genuinely felt altruism rather than only strategic pretense.
moves.warrant: Long-term mutual aid favors cooperation, while evolved detection of cheaters makes sincere caring more reliable than faked friendliness.
moves.inference: An evolutionary origin does not reduce all prosocial motivation to conscious selfish calculation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Shermer's complete answer to Vitale's selflessness prompt, including reciprocity, detection, and genuine feeling.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: when I say universal I mean amongst humans
We all get them
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale's contingency prompt ends at event 1287; Shermer owns the continuous species-relative answer at events 1288–1328.
moves.importanceRationale: This materially qualifies the scope of Shermer's objectivity and must be preserved.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies that the claimed universality is species-relative and rooted in shared social nature.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Moral universality is universality among humans rather than necessity across every possible species.
moves.warrant: Social species require cooperative emotions, and humans inherit a common suite of guilt, shame, jealousy, and other responses shaped by evolution.
moves.inference: Objective human morality may be grounded in shared human nature while differing for radically different social organisms.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains the explicit qualification of 'universal' and its evolutionary-emotional warrant.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: you don't need Jesus for any of that
objective moral values even without Jesus Christ
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale hands the question to Scrivener at events 1329–1334; Scrivener owns the long integrated concession and outsider-scope argument through event 1449.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Scrivener's crucial concession and his central limit on what secular evolution can establish.

burdenContact.rationale: It grants prosocial and some objective morality without Jesus while challenging its extension to enemies and weak outsiders.

responseComponents.description: Scrivener grants that cooperation can arise naturally but disputes that this equals universal concern.
He accepts some objective values without Jesus while challenging the kind and scope produced by species-level selection.

moves.speaker: Glen Scrivener
moves.claim: Evolution and game theory can yield genuine prosocial rules and even objective values without Jesus, but they do not by themselves secure equal concern for outsiders and the weak.
moves.warrant: Cooperation helps groups compete and readily supports kin and in-group care, while ancient moral systems also treated harming enemies as virtuous.
moves.inference: The live issue is the kind and scope of morality naturalism yields, especially whether it supports universal human rights.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The longer span is necessary to preserve Scrivener's explicit concession, the cooperation-to-competition mechanism, the outsider problem, and his final qualification; these parts form one nonmergeable argument.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: I think we are born with rights
They really are there
moves.attributionRationale: Vitale hands the equal-value question to Shermer at event 1492; Shermer speaks continuously from event 1494 through his Platonic-rights conclusion at event 1558.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Shermer's fullest account of the existence, enforcement, cross-cultural appeal, and realism of rights.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates possessing rights from institutional enforcement and grounds their scope in stable human preferences for freedom and autonomy.

responseComponents.description: Shermer answers the earlier challenge about equal human worth by distinguishing real birthrights from whether a state successfully enforces them.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: People possess rights even where governments fail to enforce them, and stable human preferences for freedom provide evidence of those rights.
moves.warrant: Constitutions, courts, and police secure rather than create rights; people prefer societies that protect autonomy, and oppressed people do not thereby consent to oppression.
moves.inference: Rights can be real in a Platonic sense and support cross-border moral obligations despite uneven political enforcement.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The answer moves from birthrights through enforcement and comparative preference to Shermer's Platonic-rights conclusion, completed by 'same uh bin' in event 1558; the rest of that rolling event begins Vitale's next handoff and supplies no scored evidence.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: maybe I'm pulling these out of context I'm sure I am
we can do better than that
moves.attributionRationale: Shermer owns the challenge and explicit context concession across events 1598–1639. Events 1629–1630 contain a brief contextual correction by another voice about the wedding-feast setting; that correction is not attributed to Shermer and does not support the scored claim.
moves.importanceRationale: This independently tests whether selected sayings of Jesus straightforwardly provide the needed universal moral basis.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges a simple appeal to biblical authority while conceding that transcripted quotations may require contextual repair.

responseComponents.description: Shermer presses the earlier biblical-trajectory claim by asking how difficult sayings and family language support the proposed moral superiority.

moves.speaker: Michael Shermer
moves.claim: Selected sayings attributed to Jesus do not straightforwardly establish a superior universal moral code.
moves.warrant: Shermer cites demanding teachings and family language, while explicitly conceding that he may be taking them out of context.
moves.inference: A biblical or Jesus-based foundation still requires contextual argument rather than citation alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Shermer's turn from historical inclusion to his direct Christianity question and preserves his explicit context concession; no score may rest on chapter, verse, or quotation accuracy.

quoteEligibleExactSpans: he is the one who so bestows value
